newsitem.title: UK: GOLF-U.S. SQUEEZE PAST ENGLAND ON LAST HOLE.
newsitem.headline: GOLF-U.S. SQUEEZE PAST ENGLAND ON LAST HOLE.

text.p: U.S. Tour money leader Phil Mickelson made crucial putts on the last three holes, including a birdie at the 18th, to earn top-seeded America a 2-1 win over England in the Alfred Dunhill Cup on Friday.

His 72-73 win over England's Lee Westwood revived U.S. fortunes after Mark O'Meara, first day hero with a nine-under-par 63, soared to a 75 and lost to a rare round of 18 successive pars by England's Barry Lane in the first match of the tie.
Then Steve Stricker trailed Jonathan Lomas by four strokes at the turn but won by four, helped greatly when Lomas drove out of bounds twice at the long 14th and took a nine.
Stricker won 75-79 to leave Mickelson with the chance to be the hero and he responded admirably.
The U.S. lefthander, who has won four titles this year, holed from six feet to birdie the 16th and, crucially, from 12 feet for par at the tough 17th.

All the players from both sides watched his final five foot putt. "I kind of like that, it's kind of cool. I looked upon that as an opportunity to make up for losing in a playoff yesterday," said Mickelson, who struggled with his putting earlier in the day.
In windy conditions much tougher on the Old Course than on Thursday, O'Meara struggled and for the second day double-bogeyed the tough 17th hole.
"I didn't play awful, it was just much harder out there. But you can have the Road Hole," he said.
Lane's round was a reminder of Nick Faldo's final round in the 1987 British Open at Muirfield, when he shot 18 pars and beat Paul Azinger by one shot.
"I had a 10-footer for birdie at the last and I tried to make it but I felt if I missed it I'd still be happy," Lane said.
Stricker birdied the hole where Lomas took nine and eventually won 75-79.
"All of a sudden I was in control," he said.

Spain beat Italy 2-1 in the other group one tie and if the U.S. beat Spain on Saturday they will advance to Sunday morning's semifinals. If they lose, they could still go through depending on the outcome of the England-Italy tie.
Second seeds Australia, despite an erratic though winning round of 71 from world number one Greg Norman, all but clinched a place in the semifinals by beating Germany 3-0.
It was their second victory and now even if they lose 2-1 to New Zealand in their third round robin tie on Saturday, they will still advance.
Only a New Zealand whitewash of their Pacific neighbours would thwart Australia.
Japan beat New Zealand 2-1 in the other group four match and can also win the group, but only if they beat Germany 3-0 and New Zealand have a clean sweep against the Australians.

For Australia, Wayne Riley beat Heinz-Peter Thuel 74-76, Norman had a six and a seven on his card but still beat Sven Struever by two shots and Steve Elkington's 71 was nine better than Thomas Goegele's 80.
Norman will take nothing for granted against New Zealand. "We were in a similar position last year and lost 3-0 to England and went out. Nothing's a lock," he said.
His six came after he missed from two feet at the long fifth, where Struever sank a 60-footer for an eagle.
Then the Australian drove out of bounds at the other par-five, the 14th, and took seven.
"It's the biggest mental error you can make. It's an easy drive there. I just hung the ball out too far right," he said.
He had six birdies in his round. "I got lax on the easy shots and played the tough ones well," he said.
Japan led early in all three matches against New Zealand, Naomichi "Joe" Ozaki not dropping a shot in a 69-73 win over Frank Nobilo.
Grant Waite beat Hashime Meshiai 72-73 but Kazuhiro Takami bettered Greg Turner 70-73.
"Japan got in front early and it was tough to play catchup in the conditions today," Nobilo said.
"All credit to them. We were outplayed."
